General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scarymommy ↗ Open Full Page

Digital Detox Gift Guide: 27 Analog Gift Ideas For Lo-Fi Fun

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2347 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From paint-by-numbers to screen-free storytelling, these picks make downtime feel intentional and joyful.
  • We started noticing it last year: Everyone seemed to be craving less screen time, less doomscrolling, fewer cheap dopamine hits.
  • After all, there’s just a special, cozy kind of magic in a night with no screens, isn’t there?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From paint-by-numbers to screen-free storytelling, these picks make downtime feel intentional and joyful.

We started noticing it last year: Everyone seemed to be craving less screen time, less doomscrolling, fewer cheap dopamine hits. And not only has that trend continued in 2026, but it’s gotten even stronger. If anything, we’re all more fried! So analog is having a full-blown moment, which happily makes for some seriously great gifting.

After all, there’s just a special, cozy kind of magic in a night with no screens, isn’t there? A puzzle spread across the dining room table. A record spinning while parents dance in the kitchen (and their kids feign disgust in the background). Coloring and baking and crafting and playing board games — comfortcore activities that keep hands busy and minds engaged.

Recent findings suggest that so this holiday season, give the gift of logging off. From paint-by-numbers to an heirloom-quality chess set, here are our favorite picks for anyone (yourself included) who’s ready to put the phone in a drawer and be fully present for all the holiday merriment.

Sources indicate that turn off the TV and start a puzzle! And thanks to Completing The Puzzle, you no longer have the excuse, “But I don't know what to do with it when I'm done!” They've figured that all out for you. Completing The Puzzle is the first-ever puzzle rental subscription with high-quality puzzles delivered right to your door. Once you finish, pack it up, send it back, and wait for your fresh one to arrive. — Kate Auletta, Editor in Chief.

I have remarked for about 100 years that I wanted to get into embroidery. Whenever I see something embroidered at an antique mall or thrift store, I am enchanted, but... they are not cheap. Even thrifted! So, why not make my own? Clever Poppy is the perfect way to get an introduction to embroidery if you're a newbie like me. In their kits, they provide step-by-step instructions as well as everything you need to get started. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

Normalize getting your mom a knit or crochet kit! If they like fiber arts, they will love it. Sometimes people gift me a few balls of yarn, which is amazing, but these kits ensure that I have enough to complete a project. I love Lion Brand's selections, and this cardigan is gorgeous and pretty easy to pull off, too! — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social.

There’s something so deeply satisfying about dropping the needle on a record. You can’t skip songs, you can’t scroll... you actually listen to an album in its purest form. This record player makes that ritual easy, and it looks good doing it with its cool retro-inspired case and little viewing window. It plays both LPs and singles, and it’s compact enough to move wherever you want. I can’t wait to hit the local thrift stores and start building my vinyl collection. (Worth noting: This turntable does also have Bluetooth!) — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor of Lifestyle & Entertainment.

For all the readers out there, this is one book accessory I never knew I needed! I throw my book into my bag along with all my other crap and typically end up ruining it with crayon marks or crumbs from my kid's latest half-eaten snack. This protective padded sleeve keeps your current reads safe from crushed pages and bent covers (and mystery stains!). — Katie Garrity.

Recent findings suggest that coloring girlies, if you're not using Ohuhu markers, we need to talk! This 104-color pack is my go-to when I'm having a cozy coloring night with my daughter. Plus, these markers have a dual-tip marker design — choose the brush tip for sweeping, calligraphic strokes, or the fine tip for details. — Katie Garrity.

I’ve got nothing against my Notes app. In fact, I use it all the time. But I will always, always be a girlie who loves a really beautiful notebook and the way it makes me want to put down my phone and pick up a pen. This journal has a hard cover that comes in some really saturated, beautiful colors; I have the Mulberry and love it, but this Deep Indigo is next on my list! Little thoughtful details just make the notebook a joy to use: thick pages, a ribbon bookmark, a built-in pen holder, and a handy inner pocket. — Julie Sprankles.

In a recent development, for the person on your list who has approximately 10,000 photos living in their phone and zero prints to show for it, a Mixbook photo book is the most meaningful and genuinely beautiful gift you can give. Mixbook is consistently rated one of the best photo book services for quality and customization, with hundreds of gorgeous themes and layouts that make the final product look intentional and special rather than just a dump of your camera roll. The design tool is incredibly easy to use, the printing quality is stunning, and they run sales constantly, which makes a truly luxurious gift very achievable. — Katie Garrity.

Anyone who has an addiction to making sourdough (or eating it like me) will absolutely love this bread bag from Keeki. It’s a beeswax-lined linen bag that stores your loaf and allows the bread to breathe. The natural antibacterial properties of beeswax will help deter mold! — Katie Garrity.

I’ve long been a fan of Papier, so I was pumped to see the brand venture into board games, starting with this gorgeous Midnight Mosaic Chess Set. It has a scalloped (!!) solid wood board with a full set of wooden pieces, plus a harlequin-patterned box pretty enough to live right on my coffee table. It’s more of a splurge than I’d normally spend on a board game, but I’m very into the idea of a set that lasts for years... something I can play with my kids now, that I hope they’ll ask to pull back out when they’re off at college and come home for a visit. — Julie Sprankles.

I wouldn't call myself an artist by any means, so that's why a paint-by-numbers kit is perfect. I get the zen of coloring, but the end product is pre-made to be gorgeous! — Katie Garrity.

For the book lover who’s trying to put down the phone, this is Chutes and Ladders with a literary twist, played on a gorgeous bookshelf board illustrated by Hyesu Lee, where ladders send you up and bookmark ribbons slide you back down (instead of snakes). It’s easy enough for little kids and charming enough for adults, with four wooden game pieces and two dice for 2 to 4 players, so it’s a great pick for family game night. It’s the kind of analog gift that actually gets pulled out and played, and it looks too pretty to hide in a closet! — Katie Garrity.

I am just now really getting into Pilates, and I feel like it’s such a top-tier analog activity. No screens, no notifications. Just me and my breath (and my very shaky core, ha). These Fraise socks make the practice a little more luxe! They have a non-slip grip that actually sticks, compression arch support, odor-resistant organic cotton, and a really cute aesthetic, too. But what I REALLY love is that this minority-woman-owned firm donates a pair of socks to local women’s shelters for every order. — Julie Sprankles.

For the adult who needs a break from wrapping presents, this spiral-bound activity book is basically Highlights for Children, but with a lot more sarcasm and a festive attitude. It has 200 pages of hidden-picture puzzles, mazes, coloring pages, connect-the-dots, festive sudoku, and word searches, all printed on uncoated paper that’s great for pens or pencils, with an answer key in the back so no one has to suffer. It’s a screen-free, hilariously unproductive gift that makes a great stocking stuffer for anyone who needs a place to hide from the relatives! — Katie Garrity.

Recent findings suggest that for the sports fanatic who already owns every jersey and mug, these books are a screen-free gift that relives their team’s biggest games, seasons, and championships through the real newspaper coverage printed at the time. They come in football, baseball, basketball, hockey, soccer, and more, and you can customize each one by choosing the cover color and design, adding their name to the front, and writing your own dedication inside. It’s an analog gift that feels personal and gets proudly displayed on the coffee table instead of shoved in a drawer! — Katie Garrity.

Recent findings suggest that these Matryoshka measuring cups just make me smile! The design is whimsical and charming, but also super practical: Each cup in the set of six stands upright, nests neatly inside the next, and measures from 1/4 cup to a full cup. They’re great for spending time baking with the kids! — Julie Sprankles.

If you want to romanticize the analog life, this is the pen that does it, because writing with a solid 14K gold nib feels nothing like a regular pen, and the smoothness alone makes grocery lists feel like an entire event. The weighty metal body in matte black was designed by Mario Bellini and has a grooved texture that’s as satisfying to hold as it is to look at, and it comes with a converter and an ink cartridge so you can start writing right out of the box. It’s the kind of pen that gets you to slow down, pick up a notebook, and actually put thoughts on paper, which feels like the whole point of an analog gift guide! — Katie Garrity.

My idea of a perfect night is analog all the way: a puzzle on the table, no screens, and something truly cozy to curl up under. The stone-washed 100% cotton has that already-broken-in softness, and the tonal embroidered leaf design makes it look gorgeous without feeling fussy. It’s lightweight enough that you won’t overheat but still warm enough for a long puzzle session, and it comes with a quilt plus two matching shams to make the whole bed look put together. — Katie Garrity.

In a recent development, nothing, and I repeat nothing, gets my family to put their phones down faster than the promise of melty marshmallows and chocolate atop graham cracker squares. I love that this Solo Stove S’mores Bundle makes real s’mores possible anywhere! It comes with a tabletop fire bowl, roasting sticks, fuel, and a bamboo tray to hold all the fixings, so you can set up your s’mores station anywhere from the kitchen counter to the coffee table for movie night. There’s even a fun little recipe book with creative riffs on the classic. — Julie Sprankles.

This is such a perfect gift for a music lover. You connect it to your phone and it displays the album cover of whatever song you're listening to. In a world where we aren't listening to music as thoughtfully as we used to, I love how this brings you back to the days when you would hold and see an album before you played it. This is the perfect gift for the millennial in your life who likes the way we used to do things. — Sarah Aswell.

Sources indicate that tried and true! You cannot go wrong with a good LEGO set, and this one is a classic in our house. I have it in a real vase on my desk, and it just looks so cute. — Katie Garrity.

It has been revealed that there is something so nostalgic and special about instant cameras. There's such a sense of joy in seeing a photo printed out on photo paper instead of collecting digital dust in your phone's camera roll. Bring this as a hostess gift to your next event, and I promise, everyone will be fighting over it. — Katie Garrity.

These coloring books are so special for so many reasons. First, the firm proudly donates 10% of all proceeds to animal rescue and rehabilitation efforts, helping more dogs find the love, safety, and second chances they deserve. Secondly, these images are based on the founder's own dogs! — Katie Garrity.

Welp, it’s finally happening: I’m late to the party, but I’m finally hopping on the mahjong train thanks to this limited-edition holiday set. Wildwonder teamed up with AAPI artist Joy Cho of Oh Joy, and her vibrant style really shines through here: The whole thing is stunning and cool and creative. Inside are 160 extra-thick, hand-painted tiles, plus dice and a Birdie Bam tile. Bonus: It comes with a six-pack of Wildwonder sparkling drinks, which are delish (the Mango Gold is my fave). — Julie Sprankles.

One of our favorite things to do as a family is family read-a-thons in the living room: We all grab a blanket and our favorite book. My daughter now begs me to bring out her adorable air mattress for a whimsical, super-cozy feel during our read-a-thons. It's even more magical under the Christmas tree lights! — Katie Garrity.

If you're looking to get your kid off screens, the Yoto Player is our go-to. Our daughter absolutely loves hers. They have hundreds of cards to choose from (stories, music, etc.), plus radio stations and special podcasts. We have both sizes (we love the smaller Yoto for on-the-go), and prefer this over other screen-free media-type toys. — Katie Garrity.

It has been revealed that I didn’t get into bread baking during the pandemic, when it was all anyone talked about, but better late than never! I adore the idea of pulling a fresh-baked loaf of bread out of the oven, and I can’t think of a prettier way to do it than with this enameled cast-iron bread loaf oven. This dark red color is SO dreamy! I also like that you can use it for roasting recipes, and that it comes with a solid-wood trivet to rest on for easy oven-to-table serving. — Julie Sprankles.

This article was originally published on November 25, 2025.

#67696. Best 'Mister Rogers' Neighborhood' Songs: 9 Fred Rogers Classics

📅 31 Jul 2025 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (780 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

Best 'Mister Rogers' Neighborhood' Songs: 9 Fred Rogers Classics

📅 31 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (780 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The anthems of Mister Rogers'might not be ones that make you bust out your lighter, but then again, maybe you should?
  • Fred Rogers was so good at so many things — rocking a cardigan, controlling puppets, speaking very straightforwardly to children— that it often obscures another skill: he was a damn fine musician, writing a performing hundreds of songs during the show’s masterful run.
  • The same is true for Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, to an extent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The anthems of Mister Rogers'might not be ones that make you bust out your lighter, but then again, maybe you should?

Fred Rogers was so good at so many things — rocking a cardigan, controlling puppets, speaking very straightforwardly to children— that it often obscures another skill: he was a damn fine musician, writing a performing hundreds of songs during the show’s masterful run. Figuring out the best Mister Rogers’ songs is mostly all about thinking about why the series was so successful to begin with. Part of the reason why a piece of kids’ entertainment stands the test of time is nearly always connected to music. The reason we still love Sleeping Beauty is because of the brilliant way Disney adapted the classic ballet by Tchaikovsky and, essentially, turned that music into a bunch of pop songs. Nobody thinks about it, but the great visuals in kids’ entertainment are almost always not the reason something is amazing.

The same is true for Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, to an extent. Yes, we love Fred Rogers’ style, but arguably, the words he spoke and the songs are the real reason the show is so enduring. Contemporarily, the descendant of Mister Rogers; Daniel Tiger’s Neighborhood, also finds its way into the hearts and minds of children through the helpful songs. And though I think some of the Daniel Tiger songs are great, it’s hard to top the originals from Fred himself.

Here are nine songs from Fred Rogers, ranked in order of how memorable and how good they will make you feel.

Recent findings suggest that I call this one the Mister Rogers version of the ’80s anthem “Relax.” Same energy. Same vibe. But, I think Fred Rogers does this concept better than Frankie Goes to Hollywood, don’t you?

It has been revealed that chances are if you’ve heard this song, you remember it from the very famous speech Mister Rogers gave when he addressed the U.S. Senate. Because this is one of his famous songs that deals with complicated feelings, it’s obviously one of his best. It’s a bit of a talking-through-it song, which is like the Rogers version of Bob Dylan impression, except every word is impeccably enunciated.

Sources indicate that there’s a Daniel Tiger song called “We Are Friends.” My daughter likes it a lot. But, the thing is, this song is way better.

Recent findings suggest that I have a very strong memory of this song, and I imagine kids who grew up in the ’80s are with me. There’s something about the sentiment of it, combined with the sweetness that really, really stick in your mind. The truth will make you free! He’s right, obviously, but there’s something more magical about it than just that. He’s right, and if you sing along, you can be forgiven for whatever stupid little kid stuff you did. Magic.

In a recent development, if Mister Rogers was Taylor Swift this would be his biggest hit single. This song is great for kids who have just learned the word “fancy,” but also for adults who need to think about their inner-fanciness. A song that is equally good for right before bedtime with your kids, or a boozy brunch with your buddies.

It has been revealed that once we start getting into the top of this list, the songs are basically great because they are absurdly sweet. Still, the message of this one has some intelligence behind it. And, I suspect Paul McCartney wished he’d written it.

Feeling safe is probably the most important thing for a child. The reason why Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood worked so well is that the idea of security and comfort was built into everything about the series. And this song is the musical version of that philosophy.

You know this one by heart. You’re humming it right now. Not just one of the best Mister Rogers songs of all time, but probably one of the best children’s songs, period. Plus, the bass player is taking it for a walk.

The theme song of a TV show is usually memorable in connection with that show and, therefore, hard to really care about in another context. Like, the theme for Knight Rider; you can’t hear it without thinking about David Hasselhoff, several buttons unbuttoned on a shirt, and a talking car. “Won’t You Be My Neighbor” is like that for Fred Rogers. If you hear you, can picture him taking off his shoes, meticulously. And the reverse works, too. If you take your shoes off slowly and calmly, you’ll be humming this tune.

What Gut Health Actually Means, In A World Where The Algorithm Is Constantly Shilling Supplements

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what experts actually look for, recommend, and see as red flags.
  • According to recent reports, nervous system regulation, sleepmaxxing, high-functioning burnout — there is always some hot new health topic du jour.
  • We’ve heard the term; what does it actually mean?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what experts actually look for, recommend, and see as red flags.

According to recent reports, nervous system regulation, sleepmaxxing, high-functioning burnout — there is always some hot new health topic du jour. While there’s usually some kernel of true health information buried in the hype, it’s hard to parse what really matters from all the social media “gurus” shilling supplements at the link in bio. This is especially true of “gut health,” a topic that feels like it has dominated wellness spaces for the past few years but also never really comes up in your primary care doctor’s office. So, what does gut health actually mean, particularly for women? What do we need to know, and what is social media fluff?

We’ve heard the term; what does it actually mean? In general, gut health refers to the state of your gastrointestinal tract and how it’s working for you, according to the American Medical Association (AMA). Regular bowel movements, no persistent pain or bloating — these are signs things are going well. Medically speaking, good gut health doesn’t mean you’ve somehow optimized your microbiome (more on that in a minute); it means your digestive tract is functioning as it should, you’re absorbing the nutrients you need, and you’re comfortable throughout the process.

“I think that it looks different for everybody, but when I have a healthy gut, I feel better overall in my day-to-day life. It’s no bloating on a consistent basis. It’s having regular bowel movements. I’m not racing to the bathroom with loose stools or, on the other side of it, I’m not going days constipated. I don’t feel that brain fog. I have energy, and I’m sleeping well,” says Chloe Melas, NBC News correspondent and author of The Girl’s Guide to Guts, who lives with ulcerative colitis, a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

Yes, it is a real thing and the subject of reams of medical research.

Sources indicate that inside your intestines live trillions of microorganisms that have a surprising impact on our overall health. According to The Cleveland Clinic, they help break down our food, support our immune systems, and may even play a role in mood and behavioral health. There’s no one perfect gut microbiome either, according to the AMA. Each person’s is unique and depends on their age, diet, medications, genetics, where they live, and more.

It’s normal to have an off tummy day every now and then, sure, but from her own experience and speaking with experts while writing her book, Melas knows there are certain red flags women should watch for when it comes to their gut health.

“If you’re having blood in your stool on a consistent basis, and that more than a handful of times, you need to go see a doctor immediately. That can look like going to see your primary care. Personally, in my experiences in writing this book and interviewing so many different experts, and just what I've gone through in my own life having IBD, I’d say go straight to a gastroenterologist,” Melas claims.

Industry observers note that vomiting, unexplained weight loss, chronic stomach pain, and difficulty swallowing are also red flags, per the AMA. Inconsistent bowel movements, whether that means racing to the bathroom multiple times a day or being chronically constipated, are another reason to schedule an appointment with your doctor, she adds. Cramping, painful bloating, or looking pregnant after eating a meal — these things are not normal, claims Melas.

Ignoring early signs of GI issues can keep you from feeling your best, and in some cases, missing a diagnosis you need. Women are twice as likely as men to have IBS, according to the American College of Gastroenterology.

“For so long, so many of us have just sort of been like, ‘This is just the way life is.’ I think that as women, we just don’t prioritize our health like we should, especially when it comes to our gut health. We’re really good about getting our mammograms and talking about our breast health. We are now finally talking about perimenopause and those symptoms. But 45 million Americans suffer from IBS. Nearly 4 million Americans suffer from inflammatory bowel disease, which raises your chances of having colon cancer. And these are things that require a doctor to help you diagnose.”.

Probiotic sodas, gummies, powders... what do experts say will actually help improve your GI health and comfort? What will actually make your microbiome happy, and what’s not worth the money? Health experts agree that a diet rich in fiber is the best way to support your gut’s health.

“I had the privilege of interviewing Dr. William Lee, and he wrote a famous book called Eat to Beat Disease. He remarked that you have 39 trillion different bacteria that live inside your microbiome and that you need this gut diversity to have overall good health, and that it really just comes down to having a diverse plate every day when you’re sitting down for your meals,” Melas indicates.

It has been revealed that it’s generally recommended for adults to consume 25 to 30 grams of fiber per day, which Melas admits can be hard sometimes with diet alone. That may mean a fiber supplement is worth the investment for you, or it may mean snacking on more fruits and veggies throughout the day where you can.

“We all get so overwhelmed; we’re constantly being targeted by drink this, eat that, take this supplement, take these vitamins. But Dr. Lee indicates that really what you need is in the front of the grocery store. It's the fruits, it's the vegetables, and that it's the things that are easiest to reach first,” Melas adds.

Ultimately, Melas says she wants more women to prioritize their health, and not to be embarrassed or afraid to talk to their providers about GI health specifically.

In a recent development, “If you are not having regular bowel movements, and by that I mean a big, beautiful, healthy poop every single day, then something is off with your gut health, full stop, and you need to get it figured out,” she notes. “If you are bloated all the time, if you feel like every time you eat that cheese or a certain meal that you all of a sudden look like you’re three months pregnant, you’re not imagining it and you’re not crazy. We’ve just been told for so long to normalize it, and it's embarrassing, and it's not sexy, and who wants to sit around with your girlfriends at night and talk about the consistency of your stools? But we need to be talking about it because, honestly, it could save lives.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You can’t germ-proof your kid, but a pediatrician states these three habits get you pretty close.

Most parents can relate to the joyous feeling of their child(ren) finally returning to school after summer break and, by mid-fall, (hopefully) hitting that back-to-school-routine stride. And conversely, the underlying anxiety of knowing it’s only a matter of time before they get sick and have to stay home. It’s a question worth asking: Is there anything we can do to prevent our kids from being a petri dish at school? I spoke with Dr. Brittany Odom, a board-certified pediatrician, mom, and trusted pediatric health educator, to see if she had any useful advice on preventing the many, many illnesses our children pick up this time of year.

Sources indicate that “There are definitely some things we can do to prevent our kids from getting sick, but it is impossible to totally prevent it. So, them getting sick is not a parenting fail,” Dr. Odom wants to first point out. She then highlighted three ways we can take action against these seasonal illnesses.

A landing routine is what your kids do the moment they walk into your house after school. Kind of like stop, drop, and roll, minus the roll. Have them immediately remove any items from school, like their jackets, backpacks, and shoes.

Sources indicate that then, kids should wash their hands. “That way, we are not tracking all of the germs from school throughout the house,” she explains. Furthermore, this is even more important for families with babies at home because “older siblings bringing illnesses home is one of the most common ways babies get sick.”.

“Your eyes, nose, and mouth create your T-zone, and this area is where a lot of germs can enter our bodies,” shares Odom. So simply emphasizing to our children to keep their hands away from this area is majorly helpful. Furthermore, if kids are apt to touch the T-zone regardless of what you say, enforcing handwashing is obvious, but worth stating again. “Washing hands at the most notable times is helpful too. So, before we eat, after we use the bathroom, and before touching a baby sibling.”.

If we can also teach kids to cough and sneeze into their elbow instead of their hands, that’s one more way to prevent the germs from entering the T-zone.

“Have a basket already set up with everything you need at 2 a.m. when your kid wakes up with a fever and they’re feeling terrible,” Odom recommends. These are the products Odom suggests having in there, and luckily, they are all easily shoppable in stores and online:.

Beyond these three tips, Odom recommends that all children ages 6 months and older get both the flu and COVID vaccine. (Mom tip: An easy option for accomplishing this is CVS’s MinuteClinic, which is faster and oftentimes more convenient than a trip to the doctor’s office.).

Additionally, if you have an infant under 8 months old entering their first RSV season, and you did not receive the maternal RSV vaccine during pregnancy, talk to your pediatrician about getting this one too. It's also approved for babies 8 months to 19 months old who are considered "high risk.”.

“Send your kids back when they are fever-free for at least 24 hours and symptoms have dramatically improved,” says Odom. As much as we want them out the next day, sending them back sick is harmful and disruptive to other students. And you don’t want to be that mom!

Since typical cold care medicines aren’t recommended for children under 4 years old, Odom says to focus on “supportive care.” These are ways to bring them some comfort and relief from their symptoms. Non-medicated saline sprays are useful, as well as a nasal aspirator. “There’s a lot of watchful waiting, making sure they are feeding well, still giving you wet diapers, and staying hydrated,” shares Odom. A humidifier is also helpful: “I recommend a cool-mist rather than warm-mist humidifier. It should be emptied and cleaned regularly to prevent mold or bacterial growth.”.

Taking Odom’s words to heart, I tried to institute a landing routine today when my 3-year-old returned home from preschool. Sure, he mentioned “no” when I asked him to wash his hands. But then, with the promise of some lollipops, he reconsidered. Hands washed, he immediately ran to my 6-month-old in her bouncer. And yes, he went for her T-zone, but hey, at least his hands were clean. I’ll take the win!

  • Sources indicate that mister Rogers knew how to talk to kids, in part because the brilliant child psychologist Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a good time to get fluent in Freddish.

What would Mister Rogers say to kids in these strange, difficult, and uncertain times? It can be hard to grasp how a child’s mind works: I’m often thrown by the way my 3-year-old makes logical leaps that are alternatingly brilliant and disjointed, with wild emotions, good and bad, clouding her perception of the world. It can be hard to know what to do with all those knotted feelings and ideas, especially in times of universal stress, with all normalcy temporarily knocked down by the coronavirus pandemic.

Sources indicate that how can we talk to our kids when we’re feeling some child-like fear and frustration ourselves? How do we make kids feel safe and secure, while giving them space to share their feelings? How do you speak to a child in their language? And, perhaps more notable, how do you understand them when they speak back?

Sources indicate that mister Rogers knew how to talk to kids, in part because the brilliant child psychologist Dr. Margaret McFarland was his mentor. Operating in the shadow of Benjamin Spock during his Pittsburgh tenure and afterwards (and whose work would not age nearly as well), McFarland focused on meaning. She understood that, to a child, a bee is not just a bee. It’s an existential threat. She offered Fred Rogers these insights and a view into the complex interplay of language and feelings, as they’re experienced by children (which she drew partly from her study of mothers’ interactions with their babies). McFarland helped rework most of the scripts for Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood and the results speaks for itself: The show has quietly captivated children for decades.

Naturally, those around Fred Rogers credited him with inventing the language he spoke. He didn’t. Neither did McFarland. They learned it, and Rogers became the most prominent American to speak it both publicly and fluently. This language came to be known among the crew at KQED, where Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood was filmed, as Freddish. It is, in short, the language of children.

It has been revealed that like any language, Freddish is not simply a collection of words. Grammar comes with it. Manners, too. It’s easy to think that Mister Rogers cast a spell by speaking simply — and that certainly helped — but it was his clarity and inclusiveness that helped him stand apart. The phrasing was always precise, not clouded by inadvertent negativity or stress. The slow pace, defined by all those pauses, allowed room for kids who were watching to think, to look, and to respond.

In a recent development, the Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood staff were so impressed by Rogers’s ability to speak to children that they wrote a translation manual. Written in jest, but extraordinarily accurate, “Let’s Talk About Freddish,” offers nine commandments of communication that collectively serve as a guide to speaking to young children in a way that facilitates understanding and comfort.

The precepts, which appear in Maxwell King’s The Good Neighbor: The Life and Work of Fred Rogers, are as follows….

The manual is an excellent tool to use when interacting with your child. I might not be able to go through the entire nine-step process or have the time — or, let’s face it, the emotional energy — to speak as thoughtfully as Rogers did. But even keeping in mind one guideline, which is what I’m starting with, makes a difference.

In a recent development, with most languages, translation is a matter of matching similar words with similar functions. Translating to Freddish, however, is about identifying emotions and relationships as well as words. The goal is to communicate a clear sense of purpose and to provide support while also introducing an idea. The evolution of an adult thought into a Freddish expression would look, in our house, something like this….

I have a lot to learn when it comes to talking to my daughter: I sound nothing like Number 9. But I have even more to learn about listening — something that Mister Rogers also knew how to do. Watch any episode and you’ll see and hear Rogers leaving quiet space around his words so kids could respond or make observations; making the most of simple, open-ended comments like “Oh,” which allows kids to draw their own conclusions; asking lots and lots of questions, which gives kids a chance to participate in the conversation and feel — incredibly, for a TV show — that the attention is on them.

It has been revealed that the pacing of Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood can make the show difficult to watch. It’s slow. But that slowness is a product of discipline, and that discipline pays dividends. Adopting that slowness and communicating with purpose is incredibly difficult, but when I manage the trick, I can see my daughter respond. She stops using her favorite daycare expression — “You stepped on my words” — and starts communicating more directly as she senses that I’m listening and not jumping in.

Sources indicate that I’ve stopped asking my daughter, “What is it?” when she shows me a drawing. I ask her to tell me about it — and she does. I’m starting to explain more clearly what I ask of her and the reason why. I’m learning to wait while she finds the exact words to explain that her play food is “hair ketchup” that she’s pouring on her head. It can be confusing at times, slow at others, but I understand that it’s my job to sort through what comes out, and Freddish helps. Asking questions helps. Being quiet helps.

For many, Christmastime is also a source of some of their best memories of a magical childhood. It’s easy to see why parents might choose a Christmas-adjacent baby name, and Noel is not the one and only option. Here are some of our favorites:.

This beautiful, classic girl’s name means “bright” or “clear.” And yes, Christmas is all about being merry and bright, but the real Christmas connection here is that Clara is the main character of the iconic Christmas ballet, The Nutcracker.

Douglas is a Scottish name meaning “dark stream.” But if you’re a Christmas lover, you’ll know that Douglas firs are an American evergreen tree species. This name is perfect if you love traditional boy names and would prefer one with a built-in nod to your favorite holiday.

Like the North Pole, of course! Kim Kardashian made the name popular when she gave it to her eldest child back in 2013, but now it feels like enough of a name that it wouldn’t be automatically associated with the young celeb.

In a recent development, if the Christmas story holds meaning for you, but naming your baby Mary or Joseph is a little too on the nose, consider Shepherd. It’s an occupation name (very trendy in recent years), and kind of doubles as a last name baby name too. But really, the shepherds in the fields were the first to hear the news of baby Jesus’s birth.

Do any of these names feel like the perfect pick for your little cherub?

#67689. The 5 Words Mister Rogers Used Most And How They Help Kids Learn

📅 31 Jul 2025 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1362 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

The 5 Words Mister Rogers Used Most And How They Help Kids Learn

📅 31 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1362 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, want to build a bridge to better communication with children.
  • The way Fred Rogers communicated has been the subject of much examination.
  • Recent findings suggest that we know that Fred Rogers created a space of encouragement and kindness, but by examining which words he leaned on, we can learn to construct meaning and child-friendly lessons out of Mister Rogers’ rhetorical building blocks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, want to build a bridge to better communication with children. Use the building blocks that Fred Rogers Used.

The way Fred Rogers communicated has been the subject of much examination. He was deliberate without being rigid. He was quiet without being passive. He was empathetic without being paralyzed. How did he achieve this? He worked hard at his scripts. In his archive in Pennsylvania, stacks of scribble-covered papers pay tribute to Rogers as an exacting self-editor. The printed scripts contain large words that were then carefully crossed out and replaced with more comprehensible language. After all, Mister Rogers, the titular character and de facto mayor of Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, spoke mostly to coma and to the millions of children watching in their homes. He understood that they hung on his every word. But what were those words, exactly?

Recent findings suggest that we know that Fred Rogers created a space of encouragement and kindness, but by examining which words he leaned on, we can learn to construct meaning and child-friendly lessons out of Mister Rogers’ rhetorical building blocks. To that end, Fatherly analyzed the closed-captioning text for 30 representative episodes of Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood pulled from the 31-season run. After throwing out common words (conjunctions, articles, pronouns), we looked at the frequency of word use. The results show that Mister Rogers was not merely a calm and affirming character. He insisted on exploration and action. He demanded curiosity. And he responded to it as well.

A breakdown of Mister Rogers’ most frequently used words provides a window into a spectacularly effective communication strategy. And his top five words by usage are a great place to start.

Recent findings suggest that it makes sense that a cornerstone of educational children’s programming like Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood would make knowing central. To know is to be educated and to understand. But for Fred Rogers, the verb was dynamic and transactional. The knowing went both ways. Yes, he wanted his young audience to know the world through the lens of their neighborhood, but he also wanted to know his young audience.

Recent findings suggest that in Mister Rogers’ world, “know” is frequently part of a question. Rogers doesn’t assume a child’s knowledge or demand that they know much of anything. But he uses knowing to pique curiosity: “Did you know…?” or “Do you know…?” has the power to draw children into discovery. The word places a primacy on the act of seeking an answer, and assures children that the world can be known. In that way, Rogers could inspire kids to be curious themselves, while also reassuring them that there was an answer to be found. Rogers is often remembered for the emotional resonance of his work, but he was not just interested in feelings. He loved to empower children with facts. The feeling of security he inspired emerged from the sense that Mister Rogers was never evasive. He wanted his audience to know what he knew.

Many viewers of Mister Rogers Neighborhood will remember the factory visits. Viewer were often taken to various spots near the WQED studios in Pittsburgh to learn how things were made. We were given a glimpse into the process of making so we could see that the things in our homes didn’t simply appear there fully formed. There were steps in making paper, or violins or rubber balls.

Industry observers note that rogers loved the idea of manufacturing. In the Neighborhood of Make-Believe the puppet Cornflake S. Pecially calls himself a man that manufactures. He makes chairs. And there are often plots that revolve around Cornflakes’ chair-making factory. Cornflake was one of the first puppets Fred Rogers ever made.

But aside from showing his young viewers how things were made, Mister Rogers often invited children into his kitchen, to sit with him a the table and craft. The projects would usually involve materials found around the home — a protean form of upcycling before the term was even coined. And happily, there were rarely right ways in which to build the crafts. There was always room for creativity. The beauty was that the word “make” came to encompass both industrial processes and creative processes. The act of creation, rather than the forum in which the act took place, was the thing of interest.

Fred Rogers was calm, measured and reassuring, yet his third most frequently used word was an exhortation to motion. One doesn’t necessarily equate Mister Rogers with action, but when you watch his episodes with the word “go” in mind, it’s suddenly clear just how restless the program is. The camera is always shifting and Mister Rogers and his viewers rarely stay in one place for too long. Again, this is very much by design. Kids do not have long attention spans. To keep his audience engaged, Rogers had to move promptly.

Industry observers note that consider the fact that the show begins with the act of arrival and ends with the act of leaving. Viewers don’t just happen upon Rogers sitting idly in his home.Viewers catch him between here and there. And while they’re with him, they go. Viewers go to factories and businesses. Viewers go to the Neighborhood of Make-Believe. Viewers go outside or to the kitchen.

Recent findings suggest that yes, as children, we sat at home watching. But we were watching a man being active. Mister Rogers modeled active behavior through the television — an entirely unique trick.

In a recent development, A close second to “go” is “see.” There’s likely a reason that the two words are used nearly the same number of times in these episodes. Because if you’re going to go, you’re also going to see. “Let’s go see … ,” is a common refrain on Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood. But there’s more to “see” than the activity that happens once viewers reach their destination. Interestingly, the word “look” is used about half as much as “see” (346 times) over the same number of episodes. “Watch” is used considerably less (59 times). What’s the difference? If Rogers just wanted kids to regard something, wouldn’t these words be more likely to have similar rates of use?

It has been revealed that not really. Watching is passive. Looking is fairly passive. Seeing is active. When you see, you notice. When you see something, an object or an event, you’ve been able to capture and retain something of its quality. In order to know something, you have to see it. Seeing is part of learning in a way that watching is not. Fred Rogers didn’t want children to watch his show. He wanted them to see inside his house and his neighborhood.

Recent findings suggest that at first blush this seems like a mistake. Isn’t the frequent usage of this two-letter exclamation more of a rhetorical quirk than a choice? Doubtful. It’s unlikely he would have allowed “oh” to colonize his sentence. There’s little reason to believe that “oh” was anything but a measured choice. And, once you think about it, the prevalence of “oh” begins to make sense. In fact, it feels kind of profound. The word “oh” communicates recognition and realization. It is a hook on which a conversation can hang. And Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood was a conversation.

Sources indicate that but “oh” isn’t just an acknowledgment. It’s a declaration of wonder and surprise. “Oh” is also “Oh!” And “Oh!” is a substantial-hearted feeling. It can mean joy or love. It contains about as much as two letters can. In a sense, “oh” can hold the entirety of the Mister Rogers neighborhood in one fine syllable.

But when taken with the other four words in Mister Rogers top five words, “oh” becomes an exclamation for a fine life motto that someone might stencil on their wall:.

It’s Fred Rogers final command to us — learn something of the world, build something useful that lasts beyond you, move beyond the places you know, make an effort to notice the world around you and never be afraid to show your joy in it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before you judge me, I asked experts what young kids actually understand and if our obsession with sexual privacy is more cultural and modern than we think.
  • My 3-year-old still sleeps in bed with my husband and me.
  • To which I say: We manage just fine, thanks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before you judge me, I asked experts what young kids actually understand and if our obsession with sexual privacy is more cultural and modern than we think.

My 3-year-old still sleeps in bed with my husband and me. I like cuddling him all night, and I’ve come to accept that it’s just the kind of mom I am: the clingy co-sleeping type. When he was littler, we took safe-sleep precautions with a bassinet and all that jazz, but these days, he sleeps right up next to me. Most non-co-sleeping families cringe at this. And then they immediately want to know: So how do you get intimate with your partner?

To which I say: We manage just fine, thanks. But lately, I’ve been wondering about the elephant in the room. Or, should I say, the toddler.

My husband and I NEVER have sex in the bed with our toddler. But we do sneak into the bathroom. Or sometimes, once he’s deeply asleep, we pull out a cot on the other side of the room and get it on in the dark. I’m embarrassed even admitting that.

I also don’t believe we’re the only parents who have ever found themselves in this predicament.

Here’s the thing... our house isn’t huge. And between the 3-year-old sleeping soundly in our blacked-out bedroom and one of our much more aware older kids wandering out of their rooms, we’ve chosen the former.

Which brings me to something else we really need to address. What about the “olden days”? Ma and Pa from Little House on the Prairie managed to have four babies while living in one-room log cabins and shanties. I guarantee they weren’t heading out to the barn or the outhouse every time they wanted to have sex, especially when bears and wolves were roaming around, and temperatures dipped below zero.

Besides, many modern families around the world still live and sleep in shared spaces.

Industry observers note that lately I’ve wondered if being horrified by the idea of parents having sex in the same room as a sleeping child is a cultural thing. Is it so awful if they’re still very little? At what point does “they have no idea what’s happening” turn into “Mom and Dad need to find somewhere else to do this”?

We reached out to experts to answer all the questions you’ve probably been dying to know but have been way too embarrassed to ask.

In a recent development, here’s the short answer: Parents don’t need to feel guilty about having sex in the same room as a newborn or young infant. An infant doesn’t have the “cognitive capacity to understand what sex is,” and they won’t remember or understand what’s going on, states Kimberly Resnick Anderson, LCSW, an AASECT-certified sex therapist.

Anderson does add one caveat, though. Having a baby nearby is likely to make parents more reserved and overall less expressive during sex. Over time, she claims, that could potentially lead to a “more permanent shift” in how they express themselves sexually.

Industry observers note that when does she recommend finding some privacy? Around age 1.

Once a child develops language and becomes mobile, she notes, it becomes harder to get it on, knowing the child could wake up in the middle of it.

Recent findings suggest that but Samantha Ridout, M.Phil., BCBA, a child development and behavioral expert, cautions against treating any birthday as a universal cutoff. No two children develop at exactly the same rate, she states, so there isn’t a magical age when a child suddenly becomes aware of what’s happening around them. Instead, parents should watch for their child’s growing alertness and awareness and set appropriate boundaries.

Sources indicate that I’ve found this to be true in my own family. We moved our older two kids out of our room quicker because they were definitely more aware than our last, who just feels more “babyish.”.

But both experts made one thing very clear: During sex, infants need to be in a separate, safe sleep space.

Let’s go back to my Ma and Pa observation for a minute, shall we?

According to recent reports, the idea of children and adults having separate bedrooms is a relatively fresh phenomenon, says Macall Gordon, a researcher and sleep coach with an undergraduate degree in anthropology who studies children’s sleep through a sociohistorical lens. She says before the lightbulb was invented, family life revolved around sunrise and sunset, with families often sleeping in shared spaces.

But with electricity, adults could suddenly stay up after children went to bed, she adds. Now, children needed a “separate space to sleep” while adults stayed up. So the nursery and the crib came along. Then, she claims, the layout of homes started to change, too, to include hallways connecting separate rooms. Before that, rooms were all connected to each other, so you had to go through one to get to another.

Sources indicate that to this day, however, a separate bedroom is still something of a privilege. Many families simply don’t have “extra, separate rooms,” Gordon points out, especially in big cities, where studios and lofts are common, or in cultures where extended family members may occupy additional bedrooms. “While we think of a separate room for children as the norm, it really wasn’t for most of our history,” Gordon shares.

Recent findings suggest that tiffany Belanger, cosleeping expert and founder of Cosleepy, notes the topic tends to divide her followers into two camps: those who will have sex in the room with a kid and those who won’t. When I described my scenario to her, she responded that floor sex while young kids are still sleeping in their parents’ bed is actually pretty common among the co-sleeping families she hears from.

You want to know if mine has woken up before.

Recent findings suggest that but rarely. He’s a really deep sleeper, and it’s only happened a few times. It’s dark, and when he did wake up, he immediately called out for me in that disoriented, half-asleep way toddlers do. We stopped immediately. The cot is also on the far side of the bed, outside his line of sight. As far as I know, he never saw or heard anything.

Will we emotionally damage our kid if he were to catch us in the act? Unlikely, Ridout notes, if parents stay calm, stop immediately, tell the child they are safe, and answer their questions in a simple, non-panicky way.

But all of this still leaves me with the extremely practical question that got us into this mess in the first place.

Parents have to get creative, flexible, and spontaneous, says Anderson. That might mean asking family or friends to babysit when you can, doing it in other rooms, or using whatever short pockets of privacy you can find.

In a recent development, and while Belanger reassures me that my floor-sex solution isn't unheard of among co-sleeping parents, the other experts think it’s not a great option when kids become mobile and verbal. So, I suppose it might be time to retire the cot. Where to next?

How To Make Fewer Grocery Trips & Still Eat Well

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1366 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that groceries cost a fortune, gas isn’t cheap… every “quick” run to the store somehow costs you 60 bucks or more.
  • It’s a phenomenon that happens more often than not these days: You run into the store for milk, cheese, eggs, and a few other basics, and walk out wondering how in the hell a small handful of grocery bags just set you back upwards of 100 bucks.
  • The reality is groceries are still painfully expensive, and plenty of families are stretched thinner than ever.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that groceries cost a fortune, gas isn’t cheap… every “quick” run to the store somehow costs you 60 bucks or more. Experts share how to shop less and still feed your family well.

It’s a phenomenon that happens more often than not these days: You run into the store for milk, cheese, eggs, and a few other basics, and walk out wondering how in the hell a small handful of grocery bags just set you back upwards of 100 bucks. Worse, you then have to play budget Tetris, moving money around to make sure you have funds for the inevitable grocery run you’ll have to make next week. Add in the gas it takes to get to and from, and you’re spent literally and figuratively.

The reality is groceries are still painfully expensive, and plenty of families are stretched thinner than ever. And, sure, cutting back on trips is probably one of the easiest and most logical ways to save money (and time, and sanity). But it begs the question: How long can you go between grocery runs without your family surviving on cereal benders?

We asked food and budgeting experts how they personally make it work.

Sources indicate that most of the experts we polled said one big shop a week is sort of the sweet spot. “Every extra trip not only takes up valuable time, but is also another chance to grab things that aren’t on the list and drive up your overall grocery bill,” states Laurie Hise, CEO of Passionate Penny Pincher.

Sources indicate that is it possible to stretch it to every two weeks? Maybe. But AJ Prasaguet, head of the iconic Palace bar and restaurant in Miami Beach, points out that biweekly shopping “can work if you have the storage space, freezer capacity, and money available upfront. Those are real considerations, and not every household has all three.”.

Industry observers note that amber Hanson, a licensed nutritionist and founder of Whole You Nutrition, emphasizes that there’s no cut-and-dry, one-size-fits-all answer. Your ideal grocery-shopping cadence will ultimately depend on things like how close you live to a store and when your paycheck hits the bank. If you get paid every two weeks, it might make sense to shop on that timeframe too.

According to recent reports, before you make your little grocery list and head to the store, open up your own fridge, freezer, and pantry. “The best way to save money is to use what you have already paid for,” indicates Hanson.

Jenn Lueke, Fresh York Times-bestselling author of Don’t Think About Dinner, does her inventory every Friday night, then builds the next week’s meals around what’s left. Example: “If I know I have a half carton of broth that needs to be used, I’ll make sure to pick up a grain, like rice or quinoa, that I can cook in it.”.

Prasaguet goes one step further. “Give an ingredient its next job before you buy it. If a recipe needs half a container of something, decide where the other half is going.” Take cabbage, for instance. It can be slaw one night, stir-fry the next, and soup filler after that.

Another tip Hise is a fan of is ordering online for pickup or delivery when you can. The simple act of skipping the aisles means you don't have to worry about impulse buys wreaking havoc on your total.

Recent findings suggest that as a busy working mom who regularly feels she has to have everything for the week figured out at all times, this was very liberating to hear! As the experts remind us, life happens. Plans change. A rigid seven-night menu is a fast track to wasted food.

In a recent development, but if it makes you feel better to have the week mostly lined up, you could follow Hise’s example: proposal five “fresh” dinners a week, leaving one night for leftovers and one for a meal pulled from what’s already in the pantry, fridge, or freezer. Prasaguet relies on a similar formula: four planned dinners, one leftovers meal, one pantry or freezer dinner, on flex night. “That gives the week some structure without pretending everything will go according to plan,” he indicates.

Sources indicate that lueke recommends starting with dinners, then exploring how you can make the most of them. “Will the slow-cooker chicken stretch to cover lunches for half the week too? Can I make a double batch of quinoa and bulk up our mid-week sheet pan dinner?” Theme nights like Taco Tuesday or Breakfast for Dinner also help reduce decision fatigue.

The trick to making groceries last, many of the pros explained, is buying foods with different lifespans and eating them in the right order. “You do not want an entire cart of produce that all needs attention at once,” emphasizes Prasaguet.

Lueke thinks about it in three zones:.

It has been revealed that andrea Woroch, a consumer savings expert, notes that some hardy produce (think garlic, potatoes, sweet potatoes, winter squash, even whole apples) can last for months depending on storage conditions as well as how they’re handled. For fast-spoilers like berries, resist the urge to buy the giant fresh packs unless you know your family will gobble them down. Otherwise, stock up on frozen.

If you're afraid frozen and canned food won't pack the same nutritional punch as fresh, well, the experts beg to differ.

“One of the biggest misconceptions about healthy eating is that fresh foods are always better than frozen or canned alternatives. That’s simply not the case,” indicates Jennifer Pallian, a registered dietitian and founder of Foodess. Frozen vegetables are typically flash-frozen shortly after harvest, and research has found they can be just as nutritious as fresh produce that’s been sitting in your fridge for several days. In some cases, they even have more vitamin C.”.

Don’t turn your nose up at canned staples, either. Pallian is a big proponent of canned light tuna (a solid source of protein, selenium, and omega-3s) and canned chickpeas, which pack both protein and fiber and are already cooked.

Just opt for low-sodium or no-salt-added canned veggies and beans, and be mindful of foods packed in juices, syrups, or sauces.

Adopting a few little habits can go a long way toward making food last until your next grocery run:.

However, Prasaguet reminds us, “Stretching groceries should never mean stretching food safety.” That means refrigerating leftovers within two hours, eating them within three to four days, or sticking them in the freezer.

According to recent reports, you should know that eating well doesn’t mean you have to buy a bunch of fancy superfoods. “Some of the most nutrient-dense foods in the grocery store are also the cheapest,” Hanson claims.

Here’s what our experts say they keep stocked:.

It has been revealed that and while many of us think shopping in bulk must save money, Prasaguet notes that it’s “only better value if you can afford it, store it, and finish it.” Hise’s workaround is to grab a few extra cans whenever they’re on sale. “A few extra cans a month can add up to a pantry that carries you through a tight month.”.

If you feel like a failure every time you serve your family dinner out of a bag or can, it’s high time you cut yourself some slack.

Sources indicate that “Frozen and canned foods that you actually eat beat fresh vegetables you throw away every time,” says Hise. Link agrees, adding, “I’d much rather see a family use convenient foods they enjoy than buy fresh ingredients that become a science experiment in the crisper drawer.”.

“A fed family is a win, and ‘fresh’ isn’t the measure of a good dinner," Lueke puts it simply. A balanced meal is made up of a protein, a plant or two, and something filling. It truly does not matter if those came from the produce section or the freezer aisle.

It has been revealed that but maybe Prasaguet sums it up best. “You do not have to prove your love through a complicated dinner,” he reassures. “Feeding your family with the resources you have is already an act of care.”.

Revisiting Mister Rogers at the Crayon Factory and What It Meant

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the factory tours on Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood show the magic of hard work and how it can make order of chaos.
  • If you were to rank the most blissed-out segment in Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, you would have a monumental task ahead of you.
  • As an adult looking back at these segments, it’s clear to me the world just isn’t that simple anymore.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the factory tours on Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood show the magic of hard work and how it can make order of chaos. If only that were still the case.

If you were to rank the most blissed-out segment in Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, you would have a monumental task ahead of you. Each show is 28 minutes of zen. But easily making it into the top five recurring warm-bath segments are the factory tours. Watching red balls take shape, pretzel dough go into the oven, the Crayola factory come to life, and a cloud of cotton getting brushed into a towel with Fred Rogers’ calm, interested voiceover makes for good television, sure, but it does so much more. These segments show the magic of work — that an object is the sum of its parts plus labor, and this process is a sight to behold. Rogers wanted to show kids that our chaotic world is an orderly place with meaning, if we just take time to look below the surface.

As an adult looking back at these segments, it’s clear to me the world just isn’t that simple anymore. Sure, the adult viewpoint complicates things (“Who’s their manager?”; “I wonder what overtime pay is like?”), But so does the world economy. Companies don’t just make a single thing anymore. For better and worse, the world just doesn’t work like that.

It has been revealed that there’s perhaps no better example of this than in Mister Rogers’ visit to the Crayola factory. The episode, which ran on June 1, 1981, sent the team packing to Easton, Pennsylvania, to explore one of the most familiar objects for kids: the crayon. The segment begins, as most factory segments do, with Mister Rogers approaching the picture frame and a slow zoom taking us into the scene, which happened to be of a great substantial tanker train. From there, colorful visual flow and fade in and out as in a fever dream. This vision is mostly beside the point. The heart of the experience comes through in Rogers’ methodical language, as if he is putting the crayons together with his words:.

Recent findings suggest that the segment, to this kid at least, was mind-blowing. It initially complicated the relationship with a familiar object, dissecting it into its essential and unfamiliar parts, before slowly bringing it back in a solid, familiar form. Out of a steaming train and molten swirling yellow liquids and people moving boxes and cylinders of wax comes crayons. This is how crayons are made. This is what work looks like. The world makes sense.

On its surface, it seems like not much has changed. The crayon-making process at Crayola is, wonderfully and surprisingly, not all that different. There’s a bit more automation. There are fewer people. But the modern-day crayon-making process (as you can see here in a 2014 video from Wired) is pretty damn similar to the one Mister Rogers showed us. It’s still visual gold. It’s hard labor. It’s how things are made.

Industry observers note that but of course, things have changed. Some 37 years later, the world is a lot more complicated and so is this crayon factory. Crayola is still be based in Easton, Pennsylvania, but its supply chain is international, its products more complex and wide-ranging than crayons, and its core value all the muddier. The quiet essence of the yellow crayon and the crayon factory producing crayons, and the factory worker making crayons is lost.

Sources indicate that there’s this plot twist in The Good Place, an excellent show about how to live a moral life in modern times, where, spoiler alert, the main character realizes that everyone goes to the bad place because the world is too complicated for good to exist. A good act, like ordering flowers for grandma, they propose, is complicated by the fact that those flowers have high CO2 emissions, the phone used to order them was built in a sweatshop, and the shipping company used to keep costs down is hellbent on union-busting.

Industry observers note that likewise, the making of yellows crayons — handfuls of yellow crayons — is complicated by modern economic forces. You can look deep into the supply chain that churns out familiar objects, but unlike in Rogers’ time, there’s no coming back to the Platonic ideal. What does Crayola manufacture? Crayons. Also, crafts, this weird springy clay stuff, animals that ooze, pricey museum-like experiences, cheap screen-based experience, slightly horrifying 5-foot-tall talking crayons, and some very colorful marketing. In other words, it’s complicated.

Since Mister Rogers’ heyday, American goods have increasingly come from far away lands and the way they’re made in those places is simply not transparent. When you see video from, say, FoxCon, the largest manufacturer of electronics in China, it’s usually exposing human rights violations, not to showing work being done. Crayons, likewise have not gone untainted. While Pennsylvania continues to be the epicenter of crayon manufacturing in the U.S. — with 13.5 million crayons made there per day — there have been competitors from factories whose standards are not as high. A massive scandal 25 years ago, which lead to a recall of Chinese crayons that were found to have lead in them. This scandal alone slowed the tide of crayons in the American market, never sending imported crayons past the three to five percent mark in America.

Crayola is dominant in crayon-making, but it is not resting on its laurels. Like most modern companies, it has expansive intellectual property. This, logically both helps the bottom line and helps a company reach more people. In the case of Crayola, the do-it-yourself craft ethos shines through in most of its products (we’ll give the middling apps a pass) and the toys and crayons offer great entertainment for kids. But the wide variety of offerings also makes companies much more complicated to understand.

It has been revealed that if you look at the latest products from Crayola this year, you will find a whole lot of things that don’t remotely resemble crayons. Newly introduced products include: Build A Beast Dragonfly Craft Kit made of Model Magic (manufactured in China), Sprinkle Art Uni-Creatures Activity Kit, and a 2-in-1 Color Chemistry Gift Set. These are not bad toys. In fact, the Build-a-Beast line are filled with great toys that require creativity, imagination, and hands-on skills. The latest from that line even made Fatherly’s hand-picked list of the 50 Best Toys of 2019.

According to recent reports, the point being, a Mister Rogers factory tour would look very different today. Crayola is no longer the maker of a single, well-understood product in one place that you can break down into wax, dye, and packaging. Mister Rogers would need to enter a boardroom, talk to product designers, marketers, and audience analysts to get the full picture. He’d be required to speak to why the company made the product rather than simply what parts went into the thing.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps most confusing to kids and furthest from the Mister Rogers’ ethos, Crayola has put a lot of money into selling its factory as a destination for experiences. The Crayola Experience, a DIY museum of sorts that released 23 years ago in Easton and has expanded to Arizona, Minnesota, Florida, and Texas, teems with smiling crayon characters on interactive screens and posters lining all the walls. There are rooms with screen-based games, “silly selfies,” melted crayon art, DIY crayon making (these are both admittedly very cool and very on-brand), and the mandatory pizza and soda and junk food you find in a kids’ museum cafeteria.

It’s an interesting place and, by all means, fun for families. But it again complicates the organization. This is no longer the place where crayons are made — a point made by the fact that factory tours are not only not part of the Crayola Experience, they aren’t available to the public. From the kid’s point of view, Crayola is a place where magic happens, a place where 100-pound orange crayons drop from the sky on Newly introduced Year’s Eve and melted wax spins into art. In this case, “magic” is ephemeral. As you grow older, it goes away. The magic of the Crayola Experience, unlike the magic of drawing with crayons, is lost on adults.

Recent findings suggest that the truth of the matter is that a Crayola Experience is an inculcation. The smiling 5-foot talking crayons replace the smell of wax (it’s beef fat that makes it smell like that). Interactive displays and oozing clay replaces sitting down to draw. Crayola replaces crayons. Of course Crayola puts its own name over its most iconic product. After all, there are already crayons in every restaurant and home in the country — what else is there to sell there?

Sources indicate that I recently showed my kids (two and eight) Mister Rogers’ crayon tour, playing the segment from my phone. I prefaced it with little more than this is how crayons were made. They were attentive and quiet, watching, I imagined, in the calm repose that Rogers’ voice instills. I turned off the phone and told my older kid she had been there (we were once members at the Crayola Experience). Blank stare. I then asked if they wanted to draw. My 8-year-old declined, no doubt feeling a little old to do some coloring. The 2-year-old, ever the follower, also declined. Then he asked for “more TV!” But kid, I thought, Mister Rogers isn’t just TV. This is a man showing us how the world works. As it turns out, it is all a bit more complicated than that.

According to recent reports, this article was originally published on Oct. 24, 2019.

#67685. Breaking: Margaret McFarland and the Science of 'Mister Rogers' Neighborhood'

Breaking: Margaret McFarland and the Science of 'Mister Rogers' Neighborhood'

📅 31 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (878 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This modest developmental psychologist taught Mister Rogers everything she knew — and then he passed it on to us.
  • According to recent reports, before Fred Rogers slipped on his shoes and a cardigan, he was a young theology student attending the University of Pittsburgh in the 1950s.
  • McFarland was already a large figure in child psychology before ever meeting Fred Rogers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This modest developmental psychologist taught Mister Rogers everything she knew — and then he passed it on to us.

According to recent reports, before Fred Rogers slipped on his shoes and a cardigan, he was a young theology student attending the University of Pittsburgh in the 1950s. There, he studied under developmental psychologist Margaret McFarland, who would end up inspiring, influencing, and actively molding Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood. To say the show would not have been without McFarland is an understatement. Over the course of three decades, Rogers and McFarland met to discuss psychology, upcoming scripts, songs, and of course, children, on a weekly and sometimes daily basis, and her wisdom is imprinted all over the neighborhood.

McFarland was already a large figure in child psychology before ever meeting Fred Rogers. After receiving her doctorate from Columbia and teaching in Melbourne, Australia, McFarland returned to Pittsburgh in 1953 and co-founded the Arsenal Family and Children’s Center with Dr. Benjamin Spock, famous for his studies on child development, and renowned psychologist Erik Erikson, known for coining the eight stages of development and the term “identity crisis.”.

Unlike Spock and Erikson, McFarland kept a very low profile throughout her career and wrote very little about her teaching philosophies outside of her dissertation and a single journal article on “development of motherliness.” But her legacy has lived on through her students, Rogers chief among them, and the core tenet of what she taught should sound familiar, even if their origin is not.

Sources indicate that when Fred first began his study of child development at Pitt, McFarland help him get in touch with his own childhood memories and feelings. When doing this, she would repeatedly use the phrase, “Anything human is mentionable, and anything mentionable is manageable.” Simply put, it is OK to experience hard feelings openly, and more importantly, when people do this, they find healthier ways to cope. This theme comes up over and over again in Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, like when Mister Rogers taught kids about how to get mad without hurting anyone, and feel many other complex feelings. It made for a catchy song and a crucial lesson in emotional intelligence, but like many of Roger’s great ideas, it started with McFarland in the classroom.

In a 2003 interview with the National Endowment for the Humanities, David McCullough boiled down McFarland’s worldview: “What she taught, in essence, is that attitudes aren’t taught, they’re caught. If the attitude of the teacher toward the material is positive, enthusiastic, committed, and excited, the students get that.”.

Rogers recalled favorite examples of McFarland putting this into practice in Stuart Omans’ and Maurice O’Sullivan’s book, Shakespeare Plays the Classroom. She had a well-known sculptor from Carnegie Mellon University come to Arsenal but told him not to teach, but to simply be excited about clay in front of the kids.

In a recent development, “And that’s what he did. He came once a week for a whole term, sat with the 4- and 5-year-olds as they played, and he ‘loved’ his clay in front of them,” Rogers said. “The children caught his enthusiasm for it, and that’s what mattered. So, like most good things, ‘teaching’ has to do with honesty.”.

McFarland championed a teaching philosophy based on love and compassion. Her friend and colleague Rev. Douglas Nowicki remembers that, “For her, learning could only take place in the context of love. She believed that if a child doesn’t sense that the teacher cares for him or her, then that child will not be able to learn very much.”.

Industry observers note that love is perhaps one of the most crucial supporting characters in Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, more than Mr. McFeely and Daniel Tiger. There were his many ways to say “I love you” and how he always let children watching know he liked them just the way they are, not the things they wear or the way you do their hair. But love may have fallen into the background or been eclipsed by King Friday if it hadn’t been for Margaret.

According to recent reports, pittsburgh play therapist Carole McNamee, one of McFarland’s students, credits her with being one of the sharpest observers. “She could just spot things. She was phenomenal that way,” McNamee shared on the podcast When Fred Met Margaret.

“I’ve never seen anything like it before or since,” Margaret Mary Kimmel, a Ph.D. professor emerita of library and information sciences at Pitt, agreed. Kimmel eventually became a consultant for Mister Rogers and taught a class called Early Childhood and Media, which McFarland helped teach and develop material for. “Margaret talked about how the child interacted with the mother. ‘Did you see her face and the baby’s face? And what about when he started to fuss? How did the mother handle it?’ I learned so much from just watching her watch and describe to the class what was going on between the mother and the baby.”.

Fred Rogers may have been the star of the show, but he never wavers from letting children be the center of attention. Even though he cannot see the kids watching at home, his gentle delivery and purposeful pauses helped them feel seen anyway.
